utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no preliminaries - there are not - we turn for a very short moment into closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness RM055. I would like to remind you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, good morning, sir. We're going to continue dealing with a document that you are probably familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we need the following in e-court: 65 ter 10971.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the English version, and the French version; page 1 in both versions. Perhaps it doesn't exist in French. So then let's have the B/C/S version and the English version. We need the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think can you see it. You can see that this is a document dated the 15th of September, 1994. You were not in Sarajevo then; right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you confirm, sir, that you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do understand it and I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see that. There it sayings underneath the heading: "Principles proposed to both wearing parties authorities:" And then, 31: "Activation of a Joint Command post settled in a neutral area. This command post is composed of three adjacent rooms. One for BiH representatives; one for BSA representatives; one for UNPROFOR operations officers." Have you ever found out whether this actually came into practice, what is written down here?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that while I was in Sarajevo, I asked if the structure was in place, and the answer that I was given, and what I saw myself, is that the -- the said structure, if it were to be in existence, was not functioning anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have your statement in French? Do you have a copy with you today?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the screen, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy? Perhaps it would be easier if you had a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... mistake. Yes, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 15 in French. In English, page 11. Paragraph 4 in French. Page 15 in English, the bottom of the page. In B/C/S, it's page 21, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is P749.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. P749, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first sentence of your response you say: "In the French army, every company has elite sharpshooters, specially trained." This is what I'd like to ask you: Who do they answer to or who do they report to, these elite sharpshooters?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They report usually to the commander of their unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, could we have the following in e-court, 10036. This document is dated the 21st of September, 1994. This document also dates back to time when you were not in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about developments in that period of time? Did anyone inform you at the time about what happened in 1994? Or did you first see this document during your proofing with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, this document was not brought to my knowledge at the time of the facts in September 1994. I saw it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, we need your statement, P749.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the French version, we need page 16, paragraph 2; and, in English, page 12, the middle of the page; in B/C/S, page 22, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You speak of that document here, and you say yourself that it was written up before you had arrived in Sarajevo. And you say -- is it correct that no measure, passive or active, is 100 per cent effective against sniping?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is right, but I do not see it in the report that you have shown me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my question, actually. Did you - and, if so, in which way - hinder the activity of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or, rather, its sharpshooters?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Yes, besides all the means, as I already explained yesterday, we attempted to protect as much as feasible the civilian population. Indeed, no protection measure, passive protection measure, is reliable 100 per cent, faced with a shooter that wants to choose a victim, a rogue shooter. So how did we proceed? We had a system for monitoring and counter-shooting system that was set up on the higher points, so these were sharpshooters that we just talked about, and we added to that another system that was on the ground with armoured vehicles, with heavy weapons, heavy guns, that were, first of all, to be mobile screens, in order to enable the civilians that were walking to go through the most dangerous places and being protected by the armoured vehicle. And, on the other side, we would react with weapon shots when shots were pin-pointed on these dangerous places. And, thirdly, we had set up fixed obstacles. Most of the time they were containers, metal containers on some sites. I should remind you that it was with setting up this type of containers in a street on the side of the science university that the head corporal in one of our units, in April 1995, when myself, I was in Sarajevo on a recon, was shot down by the snipers whose position was very certainly, as far as I can see, in the Bosnian Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly just go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "I hate to interrupt you, but my question is really quite specific, which is: Your teams were tasked with the job of pin-pointing and monitoring the Bosnian Serb snipers and not the other side; correct?" Your answer: "That's correct." First of all, do you stand by the answer you gave earlier on?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But my answer was I would like to clarify this, and I explained that my assignment, overall, was an impartial assignment, and that one of the parties was setting more obstacles on the way than the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that was not the question. The question was whether the task that you were given was of such a nature as required you to pin-point the Bosnian Serb snipers and not the snipers on the other side. And you were asked whether this was correct, and your answer was: correct.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... repeat that what I said in my answer, that this applied to the French units that were on the Bosnian Muslim side. This assignment was an impartial one, and, as regards the people on the other side of the confrontation line, their assignment was the same for the opposing party. I think this is pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at the French version, page 17, paragraph 3 of your statement; page 13, the middle of the page, in English; and page 24, paragraph 1, in B/C/S. Here, you explained how snipers' positions were being detected. You say here, in essence, that they would reveal themselves by opening fire from a certain position. We were able to monitor that with the detection and surveillance resources we had, and we could see that evidently there were victims among the civilian. So what was the way, really, that you detected sniper positions? Was it in this first way or in this second way, as explained here?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a technical question. It so happens that in 1995, which is a long time ago now, nonetheless, a time when the snipers of the French Battalions had optronic observation means, which means it's much easier to detect and record the shots in a much more precise fashion than the human eye. These specialists already had this technical equipment. They, therefore, were able to observe the shots being fired, while bearing in mind the fact that the Bosnian Serb snipers were well positioned, well concealed, and difficult to detect. On the opposite side, the equivalent specialists in the Russian battalion did not have the same modern, technical equipment. From a technical point of view, therefore, it was more difficult for them to make the same observations, in so far as they were carrying out their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The latter way of detecting positions was, as you stated, by observing victims among the civilian population. Now, would you agree with me, in line with what you said yesterday, that the snipers used the same sort of ammunitions -- ammunition as others did, and that, therefore, it was impossible to find whether a person was wounded from a sniper rifle or normal weapons simply on the basis of observing the wound?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the medical observation of the lesion is concerned, yes, of course. Other things come into play: The position, the angle of fire, and other observations of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical documentation from the Muslim side for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two remarks I would like to make here. The first is that the observer teams went on-site every time an accident -- an incident occur, when it was possible, because it wasn't always possible. And these people inquired about the incident; i.e., the position, the angle of fire, and this kind of information. And the nature of the wound as well. These people also went to the hospitals to assess the situation as regarded those people that had been injured, in order to collect medical data. That is the first point. The second is that we noticed, from a statistical standpoint, that during the period I was occupying the position I mentioned previously in Sarajevo, the number of civilian casualties increased dramatically. These civilian victims were all Bosnian Muslims. These are the two remarks I wish to convey to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How were you able to distinguish between civilians and soldiers in Sarajevo? And is it true that quite a few members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had weapons but not uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards your first question, it is extremely rare, even in this kind of situation, to find women, elderly women, men, some elderly men, or children, wearing weapons -- bearing weapons. Generally these people are not soldiers or at least I would hope so. Now, as regards your second question, which has nothing to do with the first one, there were people, of course, who were wearing plain clothes and who, at other times, could put their uniform on and join their units. As you know, this is a legacy from the recruitment process of the Territorial Defence, which stemmed from the former Yugoslavia, and the warring parties behaved in this fashion at that time and at other times also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now move to page 18 of the French version of your statement; page 14 in English, paragraph 4; and, in B/C/S, page 25, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we further continue, Witness, you -- you made an observation from a statistical point of view, and the last observation in that respect was that these civilian victims were all Bosnian Muslims. Now, apart from the question how you could distinguish between civilians and non-civilians, is your reference to the Bosnian Muslims, in your view, relevant, because, if the victims were Bosnian Muslims, the perpetrators must have been Bosnian Serbs? Is that the gist of that part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To a certain extent, yes, Your Honour. I understand what you're saying. All the victims, the identity of which we recorded, lived in Sector Sarajevo, which was controlled by the Bosnian Muslims. Among these victims, there might have been Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats who were living in Sarajevo. Let me repeat: All the victims that were identified during this period concerned people who lived inside Sarajevo. I have never had any information on victims who had been hospitalised, civilian victims that had been hospitalised in sectors which were not controlled by the 1st Corps of the Bosnian forces. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A few follow-up questions. Serbs were still living in Sarajevo? Within the town, within the part controlled by the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. There were Serbs who had remained inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you say they were all Bosnian Muslims, that puzzles me. Because if I'm a sniper, how could I possibly see from a distance of 700 metres when some Serb is crossing the street or whether when some Muslim is crossing the street? And I'm seeking your comment on this observation, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I tried to explain this in my previous answer. I shall withdraw the term "Bosnian Muslim victim." In my mind, of course, this pertained to the inhabitants living in the Bosnian Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This, having been clarified, one of the underlying issues, which is implied in the questions and -- is that the Defence's position is that the Bosnian Muslims may well have sniped at their own people. Any comment to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not feel that the Defence was putting this question directly. It is clear, however, that this argument has often been put forward. I heard about this from the liaison officers or with the contacts I had with the Bosnian Muslim side at the time. During the period in which I was on duty, I never asked myself this question, i.e., regarding the snipers. It was clear that the shots came from the other side. It seemed clear to me, at any rate, that the snipers were from the other side, pertaining to the losses of civilians in the area under the control of the 1st Corps of the Bosnian Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the high-tech equipment which would, far better than the naked eye, be able to identify the source of long-distance fire, if I could call it like that. Using this equipment, was there ever any indication that the shots that hit victims within the city may have come from within the 1st Corps-controlled area; or did the equipment, when used, always indicate that the shots came from Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the reports we received on this kind of observation confirmed that the shots came from buildings controlled by the SRK staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're now referring to reports on incidents where this high-tech equipment was used to determine the source of fire. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. The reports which comes through the standard channels, the radio for instance, yes, the reports we received, which were recorded on an ongoing basis at -- at the command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some misunderstanding in this respect. I tried to make a clear distinction between what was reported on the basis of what was observed by the naked eye and what was reported as a result of the use of these high-tech equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify my question. The source of fire is established either by the old-fashioned way, that is, where did it come from, et cetera, and sometimes it was established, as you said, through these high-tech equipment, the better equipment than the Russian battalion had -- the Russian battalion not having similar equipment. I'm mainly interested in whether, when using this high-tech equipment, whether it was ever reported that the source of fire may have been anything else than coming from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Precisely. These reports we received all demonstrated that the firing was coming from the Bosnian Serb side. This equipment, which is individual equipment, sniper rifles, these were -- telescopic sights mounted on the weapons themselves at the time, enabled the soldier to identify the shot, and these specialists could react or responded by firing on these well-identified snipers. The reports were then forwarded through the normal channels, and the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. -- well, yes, we have another five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, in such situations as indicated in Judge Orie's question, did you monitor the snipers' activity of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and did you rule out the possibility that they were involved, or did you not monitor them at all?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely difficult to monitor them. I admit to this readily, because this warring party was setting up obstacles also. I never received a single report stating, in a reliable and specific way, that a Bosnian Muslim sniper had fired against the opposing party. I never received such reports because these activities were well-protected, I believe, by this particular warring party. I just mentioned that I personally saw, on two occasions I believe, Bosnian Muslim snipers coming out from the command post of the 1st Corps of the Bosnian Muslim forces. They came out fully equipped, and I observed that they had modern and highly performing equipment, which confirms that the 1st Corps of the Bosnian Muslims did have snipers and used these also. But I never saw them in action, and I never received a single report confirming that they were out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we should go to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the break. We'll take a break, but we first go into closed session for the witness to be able to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we -- you continue, Mr. Lukic, I have one question for you, Witness. You referred several times, and I did after that as well, to the technical equipment which was available to observe the source of fire of the Bosnian Serbs. Technical equipment which was not available for the Russian battalion on the other side of the confrontation line. At later moments, when asked about this technical equipment, you seemed to refer to optical sights mounted on the rifles of the anti-sniping unit. Could you clarify for me: Were you referring only to those optical sights when you talked about the technical equipment, or was there any other technical equipment which allowed to observe the shots being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is equipment which in some models looks like optical sights but are not optical sights but optronics. So equipment that would allow the night-vision, for instance. At the time it was relatively new. Now -- nowadays it is equipment that is more frequent, lighter also. At the time it was a new thing. So the specialists in the French Battalions had, on one hand, these optronic sights which use -- was adapted to the specific situation. And, on the other hand, they also had periscopes that had the same function as optronics. They looked like a periscope that would enable the observer to be behind a screen. So these were the two types of optronics that were used by the sharpshooters of the French Battalion. And, as far as I know, I do not think, or I did not know, that their Russian counterparts might have had the same equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A follow-up question would be this. Both type of equipment seemed to require that you are already looking into the direction of where the fire came from with a rather limited angle of view. First of all, could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also mean that there was a fair chance that you would miss the origin of fire if it came from any position which was not yet covered by that electronical, optical sight mounted on either the rifle or on this periscope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theoretically that could be, indeed. But I have said that these sharpshooters were always working in twos, so two people, two individuals, one would do a general monitoring and the other one a specific monitoring. On the other hand, the corridors in which shooters that were located on the other side of the front line might see and shoot were not numerous, so you had the avenues that were going to -- in the direction of the north that would give enough view or perspective, so it was rather easy to determine from the possible areas of the incoming shots to determine the -- where they came from, what are the areas that they came from. These were monitored as a priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would now kindly ask you to try to give us answers that are as brief as possible so that we would finish as soon as possible. If we need something that is contained in your statements, we are going to refer to that ourselves. I will do that, and then the Prosecutor in re-direct, if necessary, so there's no need to repeat anything. We have -- already have your statement on our screens. It's page 14, paragraph 4 in English; and, in French, it is page 18. You see here that the Judge put a question to you. I'm not quite sure I understood your answer, especially how this is an answer to my question. "It is not necessary to go to the Bosna-Serbian side to see that it was a BH sniper that fired and that there is a Muslim sniper nest." And then your answer: "Mr. President, I would like to say that in the period that we spoke of, snipers were operating all the time. Incessantly. This is a period in which the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to unlock the grip around Sarajevo with a great number of attacks around the city. In these attacks, the Bosnian Serb side responded with fire from heavy weapons or by counter-attacks of limited range. In this complicated situation, it was very difficult to observe what the result would have been of possible sniper fire coming from the BH side." My question: Were these same difficulties there when you were trying to determine what the sniper fire was that came from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes. And, briefly, I would like to make the distinction between the areas where you had combat between the warring parties. Indeed, it was very difficult to determine the incoming and the outgoing, and the neighbourhoods or the areas that were calmer where you had no attacks and where the assignment of anti-sniping was keeping on. I would like to insist on the fact that one should make the distinction between the areas that were in military activity from other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct when you speak about the areas where there was fighting, that attacks of the Muslim forces were launched on all four sides of Sarajevo: The south, north, west, and east?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. During the time where I was on duty and in charge, the attacks from the 1st Corps, the Bosnian Muslim Corps, were directed on two axes, specific axes, from Stup to Ilidza in the west, and in the area of Debelo Brdo to Lukavica to the south. The other sectors were kept as were in the regular activity level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that topic. I thought that we could link this up, but I could not find it in the questions. Anyway, is it correct that UNPROFOR was deployed in Sarajevo in such a way that, on the side that was under the control of the Muslim forces, there were five battalions, namely, the 2nd French Battalion, the 5th French Battalion, the 4th French Battalion, the Egyptian Battalion, and the Ukrainian Battalion; whereas, on the Serb side, there was only the Russian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir. With one more point. In Sarajevo proper, the city, were deployed only two battalions: The 2nd and the 4th French Battalion. The 5th Battalion was, as you may know, in Mount Igman sector. On the other hand, there was also an Egyptian Battalion, and as to the Ukrainian Battalion, it was reduced to one command unit. The rest of the unit was deployed in the Zepa pocket. And, of course - I'm sorry - on the -- the SRK side, there was the Russian Battalion that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask for 65 ter 15746 in e-court, please. This is a document that was tendered by the Prosecution through you. It is a document from 1994, when you were not in Sarajevo, and obviously you're not familiar with this particular incident. You say that this is the usual type of form. However, I'd like to ask you something. This is the usual form with regard to sniper activity; right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no page 5 in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, Mr. Lukic, you say it is tendered by the Prosecution. I think it's the shaded part of the associated exhibits which will not be tendered, if I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It is an associated exhibit that we weren't planning on tendering, but it's on the list, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But if it sheds any light on the statement of the witness, then, of course, the Defence can use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I have no objection to its admission, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's not tendered, I will move on. And there is some technical problems anyways. Now I would like to move to the subject of Markale. [Interpretation] We need the following document in e-court: P749. That's the witness's statement. And we need the French version, page 21; and page 28 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are trying to locate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be page 16, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll dwell on this particular subject a bit longer. In your statement itself, on page 28 that we have before us now, you say the following. You say that there were several shells fired on that day at that moment and that this could be heard. However, yet again, we are going to dwell on page 51 of the B/C/S version. Actually, page 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the B/C/S version on our screen, together with the English version, and the witness has the French version available to himself, so that everyone is able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the same time, we will need page 52 in B/C/S; and page 28, paragraph 5, in English. That's the French version, but we need the English version. Page 28, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: "I no longer know whether there was one shell or two." "[In English] I no longer remember whether there was one shell or two, but as far as I remember, the shelling [sic] came from the south-east." [Interpretation] You say that you're not an expert in explosives; right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you relied on the findings of the French sappers. Through their findings, or in some other way, did you find out that 75 witnesses that were heard in respect of this incident who were on the spot heard only one single explosion?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what other witnesses said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter ... actually, we won't need the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you whether you know that Military Observers of the UN at Mali Hum -- just a moment, please. Do you know where OP-1 is? You do know where Observation Post 1 is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you call the P1, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you referring to Observation Post 1 of the UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic asks you whether know where observation Post 1 of the United Nations Military Observers was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because Sector Sarajevo had no observers on Mount Hum. This being said, I do not know the position that had the UNMOs at the time that were not under the command of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you do know or you do not know that observers from Observation Post 1 heard just one explosion?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many radars were operating at the time?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two Cymbeline radars that were in operation in the area, in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, in addition to these two radars, was there also a French radar and a Dutch radar?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both radars, both Cymbeline radars that I talked about, were French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My apologies. In that case, was there a Dutch and English radar active as well?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were the two French radars positioned?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The active radar that monitored the south of Sarajevo was located in the southern part of Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the other, please.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other one was towards Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there, at the time, a -- a system for sound detection placed at Trebevic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebevic was outside our area. We had no sound detection system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your yesterday's evidence, you said that you were certain, or believed, that the shell which landed at Markale had the first-degree charge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do know that the angle of descent of a shell, the minimum angle of descent of a shell is 60 degrees. You do know that, do you? If the angle were any smaller, then the shell would hit the building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apparently you are talking about a very specific situation, not of a shell but apparently of a shell landing at the place where it impacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, I think, it would be fair to say that the minimum angle of descent would be an angle of descent taking into consideration a certain origin, direction, or origin of fire. These are all relevant matters to be included in your question, if you want to -- the witness to say anything about it, apart from whether he's able to say anything about it. But -- you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then phrase the question in such a way that the necessary elements are there and that you also are talking about a specific shell landing at that moment near the entrance of the Markale market because that -- apparently you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the guidance given by Judge Orie. Can you confirm for me, please, if it is correct, that, according to the azimuth as measured and according to the direction of fire in respect of the point of impact of the shell which killed and injured civilians, the minimum angle of descent possible was 60 -- 60 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 67 per cent, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that? 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The angle of descent, the angle of impact observed by the specialists from the French engineering unit is, indeed, 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in your first question, you referred to the first charge used. Could you give me the exact page of yesterday's transcript? Because I find three references to the word "charge," and none of them seem to be the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I don't have the references with me, can I put that question to you again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what sort of charge was contained in the shell that killed and wounded individuals at Markale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, here again, your question, you said "a charge contained in the shell." May I assume that you want to refer to the charge with which the shell was fired. Is that what you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was lost in the translation. The charge would use -- the shell was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because -- but please correct me when I misunderstand this technical aspect - I understand that a projectile has a charge with which -- is within the projectile and explodes upon impact and there is a charge with which the projectile is propelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which does not fly with the projectile but just gives the propelling power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you were talking about a charge that was contained in the shell --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. The propelling charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The propelling charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it may be a misinterpretation, I do not know. But then the question was whether you have knowledge of the propelling charge that was used for the projectile that landed near the entrance of the Markale market. Would you agree with that question, then, Mr. Lukic? Yes. Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The angle of impact enables specialists who are familiar with the firing tables of this piece of artillery to determine that they are in the presence either of a maximum charge, charge 6, six packets of propelling powder placed under the projectile of propellant, or a charge 1, one packet of powder, placed -- propellant placed under the shell. There are -- only these two cases are possibly, and only -- it's either a minimum charge 1 or a maximum charge 6 which provides a proper explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you consider yourself to have specialist knowledge on these matters, or are you referring to specialists other than you, you being unable to verify whether it's accurate what they told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have basic knowledge on mortar firing, like any officer. But firing tables were used by true specialists, i.e., the team of investigators of the engineering unit, and this is what they specified in their reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have the assistance of Ms. Stewart in this. I'd like us to view the video we saw yesterday. It's P446. From 5 minutes to 5 minutes, 48 seconds. We will need the audio recording as well. We would first play it without interpretation so that the witness may hear what number the French soldier mentioned, and then we would have it interpreted for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the witness: For very technical reasons, we play videos with text twice. First, without interpretation, so don't worry about that. The second time you receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters say that they have not received the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. All we are interested is one number that was pronounced by the soldier, the French soldier, at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can hear that. We first play it with sound, and you're interested only in the number mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's listen to it first --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could first ask the interpreter whether they -- I take it you want to listen to the very end --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where the soldier is holding a little instrument and then, at the very end of the -- says something. Were the interpreters able to hear what this soldier said at the very end? We could then play it again and ask for interpretation. I -- perhaps I should switch to the French channel to hear an answer, but ... Yes. The French booth has confirmed that they can hear what is said at the very end. Could we play it again, and could we receive translation of the number mentioned at the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we hear from the French booth what number was mentioned at the very end of this clip?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2.800 mils.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is in English? Let me just check because I can't listen to two channels at the same time. Yes. We have now in French and in English 2.800 mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you heard the number as well?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you also heard the number 2.800?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that figure, 2.800, mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The French soldier used the NATO scale, did he not, where the circle is divided into 6.400?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a NATO scale but a scale which is commonly used by western armies because it is more accurate than a degree scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Warsaw Pact used a different scale, as did the JNA, and that one was divided into 6.000 degrees; is that right? If you know.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look briefly now at 65 ter 14118. Sir, this is Prosecutor's evidence, and we can see it says: "OP-1," Observation Post 1, "Sarajevo, 1995." Were you aware of the existence of this observation post in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this photograph before. I'm just trying to find my bearings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you observe, on the basis of -- of this photo, that you can see Markale from it? Or not.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to have taken up your time showing this photograph, but let's move on. In your statement, you say that you don't know what the intervals were between the explosions. Let me first ask you this: As you sit here today, would you say that there was only one explosion at the time or that there were several?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that from where I was in the French embassy, I heard several explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to my previous question then. Is it correct that you don't know how far apart these explosions took place?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The explosions came shortly, one after the other. I would find it very difficult to give you the exact interval between the explosions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- your question was translated to us, Mr. Lukic, as: "Is it correct that you don't know how far apart these explosions took place?" Now, explosions can take a distance apart and in time. Which of the two were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Time, Your Honour. It was correct answer. It was regarding time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, correct answer. If the question is not clear, every answer is good. The other answer would have been good as well, if you have not put a precise question to the witness. But you intended to ask what the distance in time was and that question has been answered by the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these other shells that you mention landed?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could hear, they landed in the same area, close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D565, an image.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't believe that anything had been staged in this incident at Markale. You see this man with an enormous gapping wound in his chest. You will have noticed that there is almost no blood beneath him; right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you like, yes, I can see a stain of blood on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that this man was not registered among those killed at Markale on that day?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information entitling me to say whether it was recorded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came, were all the bodies already taken away, or were some of the bodies there and still being -- in the process of being taken away?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, the last bodies were being evacuated, and people had started cleaning up the street. I can tell you that when I arrived and in front of a store which I believe is a chemist's, in front of the market, I inadvertently stepped on the severed hand of a woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've shown a photograph to the witness, but it's not just a photograph. There's text on that picture as well. The Chamber has no idea what the text says because there's no translation into English in e-court. And the Chamber has no idea, especially since you are suggesting that there may have been some manipulation, the Chamber, of course, would like to know where this picture comes from. Is it staged? Or is the photograph manipulated? Where does it come from? What is the source of your suggestion in your question that this person has not been registered? Do we know who it is? It raises more questions at this moment than it answers. But the first one is: What is the text? And where does the photograph come from? As you may remember, the Chamber has -- no. Please -- please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Since, I think we cannot introduce this picture through this witness, and we will be showing this picture more in the future. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also then the Chamber, of course, would like to know -- we have had an experience of a likely manipulated video in the past. Therefore, if you come with sources unknown to us, we'd have to find out where it comes from. Last time it was from a web site where it looked as if there had been manipulation with sound and pictures. Therefore, even if you'd use it with another witness in the future, please make sure that we always know exactly where it comes from; and if there are any suggestions about registration, make sure that we have clear information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All I can see from here is that it's coming from some Sarajevo newspapers, obviously. But [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sarajevo is a divided town to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- produce more information in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might ask a question to the witness before we forget. Witness RM055, you were asked a question by Mr. Lukic a few minutes ago. That's at page 35, just above line 8, as to how -- how many or where these shells landed. Your answered, you said: "From what I could hear, they landed in the same area, close to one another." Now, you did finally go to the scene. My question to you is: From what you could see, where did they land, and how many were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, as far as I remember, and as far as my impressions were right, I heard five impacts. When I arrived on the scene, I reviewed the impact which was located a little way beyond the entrance to the market. That was the first deadly impact. I did not spend any time on the other impacts. From a visual point of view, my impression was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I -- may I interrupt you. My question was very simple: How -- how many were they that you found, and where were they located? When you -- that you saw with your eyes. Not heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I shall repeat. I heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't repeat. Give me the answer to the question. How many did you find when -- when you looked, and how far were they apart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the first impact in the street, in front of the market. It seems that I saw the other impacts in the perpendicular street, about 200 metres from the junction from afar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go on the spot, Your Honour. I saw impacts in the perpendicular street at about 200 metres. I didn't go to the spot. There were other things more important at the time in the -- where the first impact was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you didn't go up the street. I'm just asking you how many did you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to -- to intervene. Is -- when you said, "They were at a distance of approximately 200 metres in a perpendicular street," does that mean that you cannot tell us the number of impacts at that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Yes, at that distance, no. One couldn't see. I would have had to go on the spot, which I didn't do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Mr. Lukic, I -- I have been looking at the photograph, which you did not tender, which you'll not further use with this witness. Nevertheless, I noticed that in the text the Markale market is mentioned in the context of February 1994. At least that is what I figure out from the text that appears in the frame on the photograph. And, also, reference is apparently made to General Milosevic. Now, as far as I understand the evidence we have received until now, the February 1994 Markale incident did not take place during the period when General Milosevic was in charge. So, therefore, I'm a bit confused about finding a reference to February 1994, and, at the same time, to General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding was, and is, that this picture depicts 1995. But -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what does the text say? Because I can't -- there's no translation. You have shown it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. It is connecting General Milosevic with 1994, February 1994, at Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, which comes as a surprise, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, you're a native-speaking person. You have selected this photograph. Why is it that I have to find this out by closely looking for approximately one minute to this photograph, and why haven't you done it yourself? We take a break and will resume, after the witness has left the courtroom in closed session, and we'll, after that, resume at a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First, I shall address you in relation to the photograph that was discussed at the end of the last session. I would like to tell you that I'm deeply surprised that you believe that I fabricated something here. In relation to the photograph itself, I will tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me immediately interrupt you, Mr. Lukic. I do not believe that you fabricated anything, at all. What I said is this. This Chamber, at a previous occasion, found material which, I take it by others, may have been manipulated and where you may have not noticed that, that's at least what we start thinking. There's no suggestion of any intentional fabrication or manipulation on your part. The Chamber, nevertheless, urges everyone in this courtroom, including itself, to very critically look at all the evidence that comes to us. You may proceed. I interrupted you. You would tell me what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph that is before us, indeed, the text does pertain to 1994, to February. However, as you noticed yourself, this has to do with General Milosevic, who assumed his duties only in September 1994. This photograph was taken out of the video that we watched today, P446. It pertains to the incident of Markale II. So the text is wrong. The photograph is not. I think that the Prosecution can stipulate at this moment that this photograph is from the video that we watched today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Chamber, having had a bit more time, already thought that it was a still from the video. And, therefore, we do not understand why you take a -- a photograph with text which we cannot read, which is not translated, if the video is available. That is -- comes as a surprise to us, especially if the text is then confusing. But I think that one of my colleagues even seemed to have remembered to have seen this as part of moving picture in the video. If you would -- it would certain assist if I would know exactly the P number of the movie but.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was P446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P446. Thank you, Madam Registrar. And, Mr. Lukic, do not lightheartedly accuse the Chamber of accusing you that you fabricated anything. That's not what I meant to say, and I think it's not what I said either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that's the case, and I apologise if I understood wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you why I used this explanation is because I don't know how to take stills from the movies, and my colleague was busy who knows how to do that, and I couldn't ask him to do it for me, so that's why I used this picture with the wrong text, and I apologise for that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is willing to help you. I think even Ms. Stewart would play it and stop at the right time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would kindly ask that we have 1D567 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this photograph, we see the corpse of Vehid Komar, and he was registered among the dead from the Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995. We see the date and hour when this was registered at the mortuary. Two wounds were found on his body, and there are red circles around them here. Would you consider these wounds to have been inflicted by mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally -- personally I don't really see clearly what you're aiming at with the question, but I will answer it. The corpse of person that we see here on the picture was hit with projectiles with a weapon that would be a gun, and it doesn't look like mortar fire wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one question for the witness. Could you tell us whether you are able and, if so, on what grounds, to distinguish between wounds inflicted by very small pieces of shrapnel and wounds inflicted by small-calibre bullet, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A -- a shrapnel of a shell will tear, whether it be artillery or mortar. A projectile that is shot by a regular rifle will go through the impact -- the initial impact is very small, and it will open a bigger wound when exiting, but the impact at the entry is a small hole. So I should repeat: A shrapnel of a shell or a grenade, as a matter of fact, would tear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Irrespective of the size of the fragment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whatever the size of the fragment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were on the scene itself, and you say that you supervised the investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found -- I found myself on the spot at the end of the cleaning up -- well, let me go back. I found myself on the -- at the location a short while after the impact as the -- the last bodies were taken away and cleaning up had started in my duties, after which I supervised the technical investigation and took away the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have told us what the picture depicts, the person. We see a date and an hour; that's true. I do not see any face -- could you tell us when this picture was taken? By whom? Whether it's attached to any medical report? And could we have a bit of a context of this photograph so as to better able to understand your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the future I will be dealing with this picture and other pictures a lot and that's the picture of Komar, Vehid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this picture is taken in a morgue when those bodies were processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any medical documentation attached to it or linked to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is. But I don't have it with me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please allow us to already have a look at it, since you're using part of it, and make it available to the Chamber so that we could ask relevant questions on the matter, if -- if the context would -- would trigger such questions. When do you think you could provide it? Or can the Prosecution assist in any way?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can't assist with this photograph. I don't have any knowledge about this photograph or its derivation. I do see on the left-hand upper corner that there's something in writing that I would take to mean that this something off of a video still that was part of a videotape, but I would also object to the admission of this without additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about admission at this moment. I'm just focussing on -- it says paying. Do we have to pay for it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I think it says playing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Playing. Yes, it says "playing." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: As in a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, nevertheless, try to assist? You have got the name now by Mr. Lukic. Could you perhaps make a small search on whether have you any medical documentation on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Oh, in terms of looking for that victim's name, yes, we can assist in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and possible medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness RM055, while you were on the scene, what did you notice? How many stabilizers were found on the spot; and did you see the film that was taken by the police in Sarajevo, where two stabilisers can be seen on the spot?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived on the site, I shall repeat. The last bodies and victims were being evacuated, and, simultaneously, the clean-up of the street, of the sidewalk, was being started, and also the roofs were being cleaned. I didn't see any stabilisers, and I didn't -- it was not my job to go and see what kind of stabiliser there were and the technical details. All these were left to specialists. And concerning the movie taken by the police in Sarajevo, I didn't see it at the time. I saw it much, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you reviewed the material, did you notice that these two stabiliser were marked as 12 and 13 in reports, as exhibits 12 and 13?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would just ask, I'm sorry, for a little bit of clarity about which two stabiliser and which reports are -- are being referred to. This is a very general question -- or very generally phrased for a very technical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your previous question was, among others, whether the witness had seen the film. That question was not answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now see that. Yes. No, I see it's answered. Could we -- then, Witness, do you have any recollection of seeing any stabilisers and numbers attached to it? If not, then perhaps, Mr. Lukic, we should, if it's important for you, we should show it to the witness so that we can refresh his recollection. Unless you recently have reviewed that film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did see the film taken by the police recently. But I didn't see on the spot. I didn't notice one or more stabiliser, and, even less so, the numbers for these stabilisers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. I'm not trying to stop you, but I'm trying to get organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these stabilisers, we will certainly be discussing them a great deal in the future, so I just wanted to check whether this gentleman remembered too, and whether he observed that, because he said he had been on the scene. I'm not going to go into an in-depth discussion with him on the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that 2.800 corresponds to 160 degrees in measurements? Can you confirm that; and do you know that at all?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 2800 mils do match about 160 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you read the report that you said that you read, is it correct that the investigators could not explain the deviation and that they claimed that the shell had hit a building before it fell?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I never read that the investigators, the technical investigators, from the French engineering --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, correction of the interpreters: of the engineering team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- would say that the -- this shell had hit another building before landing. If it were the case, the detonators are very sensitive and would have launched the explosion at the time of the first contact and would not have exploded later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, with regard to this remainder, whether it had been marked or not? What did your French investigators find?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean to ask, as to what was marked or not. Regarding the second question, the investigating team did observe the impact, the characteristics of the crater, and identified the stabiliser, got it, and recorded the number that was on the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're referring to reports and what explanations? Is that a report which is in evidence at this moment? Then please provide us with the number so that we're better able to follow your questions and the answers. If not, could you then assist us in getting access to any report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take a look at it. In e-court, 65 ter 10243. Now, the witness should be able to see weather this is the report that he had looked at or whether it was something different. So perhaps we can leaf through this in e-court, if you will. We can look at the report page by page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that this is the technical report that was drafted after the investigation conducted by the team of the -- of investigators, the French engineering unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the person heading the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the person who was heading the team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This was Lieutenant-Colonel Mougey, M-o-u-g-e-y, the head of the investigating team. O-u-g-e-y.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask that we have 10239 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a patrol report, UNMO patrol report, dated the 29th of August, 1995. Five mortars, mortar shells, that had to do with the 28th of August, 1995. And then, on the next page, we have number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please move onto the next page. Number 1, it says the aim of the meeting was to compare the reports made by UNMO and the rest of the investigation team. And then in parentheses it says: "(Representatives of various Bosnian authorities)." When it says various Bosnian authorities here, what is meant is the representatives of the Muslim authorities in Bosnia. Representatives of the Serb and Croat authorities did not take part; is that right.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A2, or rather 2A, says: "In the time-frame of the five impacts, UNMO and ICZ team" -- its illegible, "working on observations posts saw or heard no outgoing mortar rounds, neither from Bosnian army territory nor from Bosnian Serb army territory." You aware of the fact that not a single round was registered to have come from any side at that moment; right?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read on this document that the UNMOs who are mentioned did not hear any shells being fired. This means that one is able to check that there was OP-1, which was an observation post, which you have mentioned previously, that this was not placed under the command of the sector which was directly subordinated to the BH Command. And, therefore, these people heard nothing at all. If you'll allow me to make an observation. Given the location you indicated at this observation post, it is not surprising, given the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that it is only normal that these observers would not have heard that these five 120-millimetre mines -- shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that it is not surprising that they did not hear this, given the fact that on the 28th of May [as interpreted] other events were taking place elsewhere, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You meant the 28th of August, I suppose, because we have 28th of May in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, under (b) it reads: "The maximum angle of impact of the mortar projectile which hit near the market-place was" -- and the value here is illegible. Can you tell us, what does it read here?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I can read that this angle is a 70-degree angle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is 7-degree [sic] angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we be specific about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Subparagraph (b).

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, I said 67, 6-7 degree angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would just point out that at least the way the transcript reads, Mr. Lukic's question was -- it reads "the maximum angle of impact...," and I believe when we zoomed in on (b), which is where the witness went to, that reads the minimum angle of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in the translation it says "the maximum." There may be a translation issue there. Could we have a closer look at the original handwritten version on paragraph (b). Mr. Lukic, it -- it looks as if there is a -- as if there is a translation error. In the original, it says the minimum angle of, and I'm not a B/C/S-speaking person, but it very much looks as if it says "maximum." Now, usually, the angle of impact, taking into account the surrounding buildings, results in a minimum rather than in a maximum. However, of course, there's also still the pattern of the impact on the ground, which may shed some light on the -- on the angle of descent as well, although with less precision usually. Is it sufficiently corrected here? I, nevertheless, would like to have a better translation in B/C/S, not because the Chamber will rely on it but to have a complete and accurate record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that at an angle of 67 degrees, as an angle of descent of a shell, and with charge 1, when the shell is fired, the distance between the point from which the shell was fired and the point of impact is 1.000 metres or less? Do you have knowledge that would enable you to either confirm or deny this?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I deny this statement. The specialists who are familiar with the firing tables used by artillery men with this type of equipment indicate that for a minimum charge, the minimum range is 1.300 metres, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the maximum range? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum range of -- for this type of weapon would be 8 to 9 kilometres. Let me specify, with the maximum propelling charge, i.e., charge 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't precise enough again. We are talking about military issues, after all. What would the maximum range be for a shell propelled with charge 1 and considering that the angle of descent is 67 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that my technical knowledge does not go that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you anyway. Mine would be even less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question in this respect. I take it that you need the tables to interpret the range of -- or at least the trajectory, to establish them. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one should be able to read the corresponding firing tables and, of course, it would be useful for somebody accustomed to reading these firing tables to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the place from where the projectile was fired and where it landed, would that have an impact on the distance such a projectile travels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour. Not on the characteristics of the trajectory itself but on the distance, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will conclude this topic soon, but let me ask you this: Is it true that you and General Smith decided to advance a theory whereby the charge used was charge 1 as that would have justified a NATO strike?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interpretation which only you can commit to and I do not share this interpretation, and I can explain to you why. Even if contrary to what you've asked me to do, I would provide you with a rather lengthy answer. The conclusions I presented to General Smith, conclusions which he endorsed, was that the projectile, the deadly projectile, could have only have been fired with a propelling charge 1 because the angle of impact was consistent with the firing tables which our specialists had given us, that's the first point. And second point, the trajectory radar, Cymbeline, which was located to the south of the airport, which you have mentioned, detected no trajectory whatsoever. Therefore, the projectile flew below the monitoring range of the equipment. If the projectile had been fired with a propelling -- with a maximum propelling charge, it would have, in its ascending period, and descending period, it would have crossed the radar -- the range of the radar, the purpose of which is to detect artillery fire. The radar provided no information whatsoever. The projectile, therefore, flew below the range of the radar. So it was, indeed, the minimum -- minimum charge 1 which was used. That said, we did have questions on the consequences of this statement and as part of the military/political context at the end of the month of August. We knew that these conclusions would have dire consequences. We did think about it and weigh up our conclusions and we -- I personally felt, and this was shared by General Smith, that this had to be put down on paper and signed, and we did this in full responsibility and not lightheartedly at all, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how far away was the confrontation line in Sarajevo when you draw a line to the point where possibly the shell was fired from?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the entrance of the Markale market on the azimuth line, the confrontation line was between 800 and 1.000 metres from the point of impact at the entrance of the Markale market. Between 800 and 1.000 metres. In other words, if fired with a minimum charge, charge 1, the artillery piece could have been at a bare minimum from -- landed from 300 to 500 metres from the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
